catalog_quote: Tone is distinctive in Logba. Two tones are identified in the lexical data compiled on Logba. High tone is marked ( ́) and Low tone is unmarked. A third tone, Rising tone is phonetically realised on a single syllable peak and is represented as ( ̌). This tone is found on a limited number of borrowed words from Ewe with the inland Ewe dialect tone (see 82). Tone is realised on vowels and syllabic nasals. The meaning of a word depends on the tone of each syllable as well as the vowels and consonants of which the word is made. ... Monosyllabic words can either be Low tone or High tone. ... All possible tonal patterns, LL, HH, LH, and HL, are attested in disyllabic roots. ... English is a stress-timed language and has syllable types which are not found in the Logba language. new_statements.quote: Ch. 4 abstract: "A typologically rare pattern typifies Ikpana declarative intonation—at the right edges of Intonational Phrases, Low tones are depressed and a High/Mid tone reversal takes place. In polar questions, final High and Mid tones maintain their lexical tones, edge-final Low tones rise to sub-Mid levels, and final vowels are lengthened." Ch. 1 abstract: "The chapter sketches a basic overview of the grammar, touching on aspects that will be relevant in later chapters, and concludes with a preview of the findings presented in the remaining chapters of the book."

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Dorvlo-2008-based record (lexical tone language, no word stress or accent described). Adds, at the abstract level, that the lexical tone inventory is three-level (High/Mid/Low) rather than the two-level H/L system Dorvlo 2008 describes, and gives the tonal shape of declarative vs. interrogative intonation at Intonational Phrase edges. No stress statement, so the catalog's stress reading is unchanged.
new_statements.rule_in_words: From the abstracts only: Ikpana has lexical tones at three levels (High, Mid, Low) and its sentence prosody is described entirely in terms of those lexical tones at Intonational Phrase edges (L depression, H/M reversal in declaratives; final H/M maintained, final L raised, final vowel lengthened in polar questions). Nothing in the abstracts of chs. 1, 4 or 5, or in the book abstract, mentions word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: not mentioned; ch. 4 abstract notes wh-questions lack final lengthening and keep final Low tones Low (intonation, not stress)
new_statements.identity_note: The book is explicitly about Ikpana "also known as Logba" (book abstract), i.e. Glottolog logb1245; the ch. 1 abstract says the chapter discusses "the dialects of Ikpana" but nothing readable identifies which dialect the book's consultants speak. Dorvlo 2008 (catalog source) is titled A Grammar of Logba (Ikpana); same language.

Glottolog lists no competing grammar (the 1953 Dorvlo entry is a mis-dated duplicate; Westermann 1903 is an 18-pp sketch). sources.quote: direct download-extracted: 'Ikpana, like other Kwa languages (and most West African languages), has lexical tones (three level tones, which is typical for GTM).' Ch. 4 reports controlled production experiments with pitch tracks: interrogatives end higher than declaratives, declaratives show downstep/upstep and H/M 'tone reversal', yes/no questions show final vowel lengthening. No mention of word stress or accent.
